client: I’ve been really on edge thinking about this family reunion coming up. My cousin always makes these backhanded comments about how I "still haven’t settled into a real career" in front of the whole family, and it makes me feel so small. I don’t even want to go, but skipping it would just give them more ammunition to talk about me.
therapist: It sounds like you're feeling really conflicted—on one hand dreading the hurtful comments, but on the other hand feeling trapped because skipping the event might make things worse. What thoughts come up when you imagine yourself in that situation with your cousin?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I immediately picture myself frozen at the dinner table while everyone laughs at her "jokes" about me. My chest gets tight thinking about it, and I keep telling myself "They all think I'm a failure" even though logically I know that's probably not true for everyone there.
therapist: It sounds like this situation feels really overwhelming—your body is reacting strongly to just imagining it. Let’s unpack that thought "They all think I'm a failure." What evidence do you have that supports or challenges that belief?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, moderate-paced speech

client: Well, my aunt always changes the subject when my cousin starts in on me, and last year my brother actually told her to knock it off. But then I think about how no one ever stands up for me directly, and my parents just give me that disappointed look afterward. It makes me feel like they're all just tolerating me.
therapist: You're noticing some people do show care in their own ways, but it still hurts that the support isn't more direct. That "disappointed look" from your parents—what do you imagine they're disappointed about in that moment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think they're disappointed that I don't defend myself more. Like I should be able to just laugh it off or give some witty comeback, but I just shut down. And part of me worries they're actually agreeing with my cousin, like they think I should have my life more together by now too.
therapist: I hear how much pain this causes you—your voice is carrying a lot more hurt than your words alone suggest. You're holding two heavy thoughts: that you should defend yourself better, and that your family might secretly agree with your cousin. Which of these feels most painful to you right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: The thought about my family secretly agreeing hurts worse, because at least the part about not defending myself feels like something I could theoretically change. But if they really think I'm a failure... I don't know how to fix that. It makes me feel completely alone, even when I'm surrounded by them.
therapist: That fear of being fundamentally seen as a failure by the people who matter most—that cuts deep. I notice your voice sounds smaller and quicker when you talk about this, like the pain is rushing out. What would it feel like to test that belief—that they see you as a failure—by having one honest conversation with the family member you trust most?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I think about talking to my brother about it, but then I imagine him just brushing it off like "Oh you know how she is" and not really understanding how much it hurts. Plus if I bring it up and he doesn't respond the way I hope, then I'll have proof they all really do think badly of me, and that terrifies me.
therapist: You're caught between needing support and fearing confirmation of your worst fears—that's an incredibly vulnerable place to be. I notice you're speaking very quietly about this—what do you imagine would be the absolute worst outcome if your brother did respond by brushing it off?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: The worst would be realizing my entire family actually sees me as the family joke. That they've all been pitying me behind my back this whole time. The thought makes me want to never see any of them again, which is terrifying because they're all I have.
therapist: Your voice sounds really urgent and pained as you describe this—it's clear how deeply this fear goes for you. Let's slow down for a moment: what makes you so certain your family sees you this way, versus this being your inner critic speaking for them?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: I guess... when I really think about it, no one's ever actually said I'm a failure except my cousin. But their silence when she talks feels like agreement. Maybe part of me knows I'm projecting my own doubts onto them, but that doesn't make the hurt any less real.
therapist: You're making such an important distinction here—recognizing that your cousin's voice might be amplifying your own inner doubts. The pain is still real, but now you're starting to separate what's actually being said from what you fear might be thought. How does it feel to name that difference out loud?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: It feels... shaky but kind of relieving, like maybe I'm not completely crazy for feeling this way. But now I'm stuck wondering - if most of this is in my head, why does it hurt so damn much every single time? That doesn't go away just because I realize it might be exaggerated.
therapist: You're holding two important truths at once—that the pain is very real, and that your thoughts might be intensifying it. That frustration about why the hurt persists even with this new awareness—can you tell me more about what that frustration feels like in your body right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: It's like a tight knot in my stomach that won't undo, and my hands feel shaky. The worst part is my brain keeps cycling between "You're overreacting" and "No, this is real pain" - which just makes me feel more exhausted and hopeless about ever feeling better.
therapist: That physical tension and mental back-and-forth sounds exhausting—like your body and mind are locked in this painful tug-of-war. When you notice that tight knot in your stomach, does it feel more like the physical manifestation of your thoughts, or does it seem to have a life of its own?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech
